plan.contextChunk: This figure stacks three waveform traces on a shared horizontal time axis to compare two ways of encoding a message on a radio carrier. The topmost trace is a smooth black curve with two broad crests separated by a single trough, labeled Signal at its right end; it is the slowly varying information waveform. Below it a red trace labeled AM oscillates far more rapidly, with the spacing between successive peaks held uniform while their height swells and shrinks: the excursion from peak to trough is largest beneath the two crests of the black curve and collapses to its smallest beneath the black trough, so the outline traced by the red peaks reproduces the shape of the signal above it. The lowest trace, drawn in blue and labeled FM, keeps a constant peak-to-trough height clear across the page while its cycles bunch tightly together below the signal crests and stretch apart below the signal trough. Setting the two carriers one beneath the other invites a direct comparison of which wave property carries the information, envelope height in one case and cycle spacing in the other. The drawing accompanies the treatment of the radio region of the electromagnetic spectrum, where amplitude modulation and frequency modulation are distinguished as the two schemes used to broadcast a signal.

interactionPlan.concept: Amplitude modulation and frequency modulation encode the same slowly varying message onto a fast carrier by varying two different wave properties — the AM envelope's height and the FM cycle spacing — so a receiver must read the correct property to recover the original signal.
elements: shared horizontal time axis (implicit, faint baseline) common to all three traces
top trace: smooth black low-frequency 'Signal' curve with two broad crests and one trough between them, labeled 'Signal' at right
middle trace: red high-frequency 'AM' carrier whose peak-to-trough height swells under the signal crests and collapses under the signal trough, labeled 'AM' at right
dashed red envelope outline tracing the AM peak heights (reproduces the signal shape)
bottom trace: blue high-frequency 'FM' carrier of constant peak-to-trough height whose cycles bunch tightly under signal crests and stretch apart under the signal trough, labeled 'FM' at right
vertical scan marker (time cursor) spanning all three traces
readout panel reporting, at the cursor instant: signal height, AM envelope height, and FM local cycle spacing (or instantaneous frequency)
reconstructed/extracted black signal curve overlaid above the active carrier when decoding is shown

interactions.label: Time
interactions.teaches: At any single instant the AM envelope height equals the signal value while the FM cycle spacing (inverse of local frequency) equals it — so the message lives in amplitude for AM and in frequency for FM, even though both carriers look like fast wiggles

interactions.label: Decode carrier
interactions.teaches: Reading the right property from either carrier reconstructs the identical original signal: the AM envelope height and the FM cycle density both trace out the same black curve, proving the two schemes carry the same information in different wave properties

demo_steps.title: The message to send
demo_steps.narration: The top black curve is the information (the 'Signal'); the red and blue traces below are fast carriers that will hide this message inside them. Park the cursor on a crest and note the signal is high here.

demo_steps.title: AM hides it in height
demo_steps.narration: Drag the cursor to the trough: the red AM wave's peak-to-trough height shrinks to its minimum exactly where the signal is lowest, and its dashed envelope redraws the signal shape — amplitude is doing the carrying.

demo_steps.title: FM hides it in spacing
demo_steps.narration: Switch to FM and keep the cursor at the trough: the blue wave's height is unchanged, but its cycles are now stretched far apart — the message has moved into frequency (cycle spacing) instead of amplitude.

demo_steps.title: Same message, two encodings
demo_steps.narration: Move the cursor to a crest under FM: cycles bunch tight and the reconstructed black signal above the blue trace matches the original. Decoding either carrier by reading its correct property recovers the very same signal.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: AM and FM transmit the identical message by modulating two different properties of the carrier — amplitude versus frequency — so the receiver must extract the matching property to recover the original signal.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Stack three horizontal waveform traces with generous vertical gaps on a common time span; label each at its right end ('Signal' black, 'AM' red/orange, 'FM' blue). Signal: ~1.5 cycles of a slow sinusoid (two crests, one central trough). AM: dense carrier whose amplitude envelope follows the signal — draw a faint dashed envelope through the red peaks so the eye sees the signal shape reappear. FM: dense carrier of strictly constant amplitude whose local wavelength shortens under the signal crests and lengthens under the trough. Add a thin vertical scan line crossing all three traces driven by the Time slider, with a small readout box listing signal height, AM envelope height, and FM cycle spacing at that x. When the toggle selects a carrier, dim the other carrier slightly and overlay a reconstructed black signal curve just above the active one to visualize decoding. Keep colors high-contrast (black/red/blue on white) and the three traces visually aligned in time so the envelope/spacing correspondence is obvious.

authoredContext:
Many valuable technologies operate in the radio (3 kHz-300 GHz) frequency region of the electromagnetic spectrum. At the low frequency (low energy, long wavelength) end of this region are AM (amplitude modulation) radio signals (540-2830 kHz) that can travel long distances. FM (frequency modulation) radio signals are used at higher frequencies (87.5-108.0 MHz). In AM radio, the information is transmitted by varying the amplitude of the wave (the figure). In FM radio, by contrast, the amplitude is constant and the instantaneous frequency varies.

This schematic depicts how amplitude modulation (AM) and frequency modulation (FM) can be used to transmit a radio wave.

This figure shows 3 wave diagrams. The first wave diagram is in black and shows two crests, indicates a consistent distance from peak to trough, and has one trough in its span across the page. The label, “Signal,” appears to the right. Just below this, a wave diagram is shown in red. The wave includes sixteen crests, but the distance from the peaks to troughs of consecutive waves varies moving across the page. The peak to trough distance is greatest in the region below the peaks of the black wave diagram, and the distance from peak to trough is similarly least below the trough of the black wave diagram. This red wave diagram is labeled, “A M.” The third wave diagram is shown in blue. The distance from peak to trough of consecutive waves is constant across the page, but the peaks and troughs are more closely packed in the region below the peaks of the black wave diagram at the top of the figure. The peaks and troughs are relatively widely spaced below the trough region of the black wave diagram. This blue wave diagram is labeled “F M.”

Other technologies also operate in the radio-wave portion of the electromagnetic spectrum. For example, 4G cellular telephone signals are approximately 880 MHz, while Global Positioning System (GPS) signals operate at 1.228 and 1.575 GHz, local area wireless technology (Wi-Fi) networks operate at 2.4 to 5 GHz, and highway toll sensors operate at 5.8 GHz. The frequencies associated with these applications are convenient because such waves tend not to be absorbed much by common building materials.
